copy_rules: Write plain, confident American English. Active voice, second person (you, your team).
Lead with the benefit, not the feature or the company history. The headline states the outcome in under 8 words.
One idea per scene. Cut qualifiers, filler and corporate phrasing; no 'cutting-edge', 'revolutionary' or 'world-class' unless a source says it.
Use specific numbers and named customers when sourced; prices in USD only if a source gives them.
Write the product name exactly as the brand writes it in Latin letters.
Keep each narration line under 18 words so it reads in about 5 seconds.
End with a direct, action-first call to action such as 'Start free' or 'Book a demo'.
style_rules: Sparser than a Japanese page: one bold headline and at most two short supporting points per scene, lots of whitespace.
Bold, large headline (88 to 110px, weight 800) with tight tracking; supporting text 36px, weight 500.
Use the brand's own colors with one accent color for emphasis; Inter for all text.
Show proof as a single strong number, logo strip or quote rather than a list.
Confident, snappy motion: 250 to 400ms eases, quick cuts, no clutter.
End on the logo, a single call-to-action button and the URL.

buyer_persona.title_en: Head of international expansion at a software company planning a Japan launch
cares_about: Whether the output is truly local, not a translation
Evidence: every claim traceable to a source
Speed and cost compared with hiring a local agency
What the tool cannot do, stated plainly

questions.q: Does it read like native, confident US B2B copy with no hype or translation artifacts?
Are accuracy and honesty concerns addressed with evidence?
Is there concrete proof that matters to a company entering Japan, such as how local review works, sourced facts, or real example runs?
Is it clear in seconds what the product does for my team and what to do next?
